item.title: Modern theatrics of love: desires and consumption in the Indian middle class
item.dc:creator: Parul Bhandari
item.description: This article analyses class construction amongst the urban Indian middle class, through a novel prism of romantic love, specifically performances of romantic love which in turn highlight anxieties of being middle class. The article explains how a performance of romantic love before marriage is used as a basis by the middle class to claim being global and modern. This is argued by putting forth what the article calls the modern theatrics of love, that is, performing and articulating romantic love in perfectly curated and globally recognized ways that are popularized by professionals (wedding planners, photographers, the hospitality industry) and the media. The context in which modern theatrics of love is explained is of neoliberal India as this article unpacks the entanglements of consumerism, love, and marriage. It further explains how the modern theatrics of love is practised by couples that base their marriage on love as well as those who have an arranged marriage. As such, this article argues that while previous works have emphasized the place of love in marriage for construction of a class identity, there is now also an emphasis on performing of love before marriage in specific ways that are intelligible to a global audience.

item.title: The role of the Eastern Mediterranean in human evolution: recent results from Greece
item.dc:creator: Katerina Harvati
item.description: The Eastern Mediterranean lies directly on the principal migration route for human groups dispersing across Africa, Europe, and Asia. It also encompasses the Balkans, where fauna and flora, as well as hominin populations, are thought to have persisted through glacial periods. Based on this geographic position, the region's palaeoanthropological record would be expected to be among the longest and most continuous, but also the most highly diverse, reflecting complex processes of late survivals, new arrivals, and, potentially, contact between different lineages. While the record from the Near East meets these expectations, little evidence exists to support them in the northern part of the Easter Mediterranean. Here I present new evidence from our recent work in Greece, both in the laboratory and in the field. These new data highlight the regions’ importance as both dispersal corridor and glacial refugium for human populations in the Pleistocene. Results strongly suggest that the paucity of currently available data is due to lack of research, and highlight the potential of the record to shed further light on the complex processes underlying human evolution and dispersals.

item.title: Comment by Paul Robert Gilbert
Islam at the monastery: on infinity as subtractive truth
item.dc:creator: Aaron F. Eldridge
item.description: Based on ethnographic research at Rūm Orthodox Christian monasteries in Lebanon, the article studies scenes of Islam at the monastery as they intersect with anxious public debates on, and anthropological theorizations of, sectarianism and ‘Muslim–Christian’ relations in the Mashriq. The article demonstrates that these monastics, when speaking about Islam's imbrication with Orthodox Christianity, defer the desire for mediation and thus effect truth as what is neither language nor body. What subsequently appears is an element permanently exempted from sociological or theological mediation – points of actual infinity. To prove this, the article utilizes two modes of thinking: the so‐called ‘apophatic’ tradition of Orthodox theology and modern mathematical set theory.

item.title: The Swanscombe fossil at 90: revisiting its phylogeny, taxonomy, and place in human origins
item.dc:creator: Emma E. Bird; Chris Stringer
item.description: The year 2025 marked the ninetieth since a fossil hominin occipital bone was discovered in Swanscombe, southeast England. In subsequent years, its parietal bones were found, producing what remains the oldest partial cranium from Britain today. In the earliest analyses, it was interpreted as a descendant of the infamous fraudulent fossil Piltdown Man and evidence for the deep antiquity of Homo sapiens in Europe. Eventually, its affinity to Neanderthals was recognized, although its taxonomic attribution remains contentious. The evolving interpretation of Swanscombe over the past ninety years reflects the history of human origins research and highlights many of its challenges, including how factors such as geopolitics influence scientific interpretation. Today, in light of larger and more complete fossil assemblages, Swanscombe is sometimes a footnote in research; however, its age, location, and combination of morphological traits distinguish it among the Middle Pleistocene European fossils. Future comparisons to the similarly aged Sima de los Huesos assemblage in Spain would be particularly valuable for advancing our understanding of within‐species diversity during the Middle Pleistocene.

item.title: Vital events, vital relations: the structure of relations in an identity database
item.dc:creator: Zehra Hashmi
item.description: The National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) manages Pakistan's biometric‐based national identity database, one of the largest identification systems of its kind in the world. This article examines bureaucratic practices used during identity registration to record ‘vital events’ in the lives of citizens: birth, marriage, divorce, and death. Through an ethnographic study of NADRA's Identity Registration Centre in Islamabad, it illustrates how Pakistan's identification system uses vital events to create ‘vital relations’ by linking individuals to their next of kin. It argues that the way citizens negotiate vital event registration reveals the dynamic nature of kinship, both lived and datafied, as kin relations are continually reconstructed within the identity database. The system does so by drawing lines of descent from both parents according to a cognatic logic in order to establish individual identity. This cognatic logic represents a shift in longstanding modes of recording kinship by both the Pakistani state and the colonial state that preceded it. This article illuminates the multi‐faceted implications of such a shift, delineating how ordinary citizens navigate their datafied kin networks alongside their lived relations at the Registration Centre.

item.title: The emergence and complexification of symbolic practices in the Homo lineage: an archaeological and cognitive perspective
item.dc:creator: Francesco d'Errico; Ivan Colagè; Larissa M. Straffon; Andrea Bender
item.description: Recent archaeological discoveries, reviewed in this essay, challenge traditional views on the emergence of human symbolic cognition. Once believed to have originated in Europe around 40,000 years ago, new evidence shows it emerged much earlier across diverse regions. Geometric engravings from Blombos Cave in South Africa date back 77,000 years, while body ornaments over 140,000 years old have been found in North Africa, with similar artifacts from Africa and the Middle East ranging from 120,000 to 70,000 years ago. Human remains from Africa suggest a gradual accretion of modern anatomical traits starting 300,000 years ago, challenging the idea of a sudden cognitive leap due to speciation. Neanderthals also displayed symbolic behaviours such as using pigments, creating ornaments, engravings, burials, and symbolic cave spaces. Evidence of interbreeding between Upper Pleistocene Homo populations further indicates that symbolic cognition was not unique to Homo sapiens . These findings suggest that cognitive evolution was a gradual process shaped by regional ecological and cultural dynamics. This novel view on the emergence of symbolic cognition underscores the role of cultural transmission and niche construction in the development of symbolic capacities, rather than a single species‐specific event.

item.title: When sharing becomes shameful: atmospheres of class formation in Namibia
item.dc:creator: Michael Schnegg
item.description: Anthropologists have long shown that asking for food in times of need is morally valued in rural Namibia. Yet among the Damara pastoralists with whom I work, people now increasingly describe feeling shame ( taob ) when they ask for food. In this article, I trace this shift to the affective dynamics of social class formation. Whereas dependence on others was historically affirmed as good, independence has become the salient norm. Under conditions of rising inequality, being seen in need thus easily turns into a source of shame. Sartre's account of the hurtful gaze is a familiar tool for analysing such moments. However, in rural Namibia the lines between ‘haves’ and ‘have‐nots’ remain blurred, and empowering, empathetic gazes continue to unsettle emerging class boundaries. My theorizing points to this duality of the gaze and the way class formation shapes atmospheres in which sharing increasingly becomes shameful.

item.title: Cutting freedom down to size
item.dc:creator: Harri Englund
item.description: Freedom, as a concept and a value, presents limited prospects for anthropological comparison. The study of enslavement, much neglected in attempts to develop an anthropology of freedom, shows that freedom has been imagined by the enslaved as the opposite of their condition only under particular circumstances. An exploration of vernacular opposites to enslavement reveals obligations rather than freedom as having the potential to expand the scope of anthropological comparison. Drawing on both literary sources and fieldwork, a conceptual history of the Chichewa language in south‐central Africa uncovers interlocking semantic fields in which some lexical items predate the long‐distance slave trade, while others derive from the language of the nineteenth‐century slavers. Obligations appear not only as constraints but also as subjects of contentious claims within unequal relationships, coexisting with contemporary claims for personal freedom. As such, attention to obligations can advance topics of current anthropological interest – such as care and hospitality – in a way that is faithful to vernacular concepts and concerns.

item.title: The morphological affinities of the fossil cranium from Kabua, Kenya
item.dc:creator: Abel Marinus Bosman; Laura Tabitha Buck; Hugo Reyes‐Centeno; Marta Mirazón Lahr; Chris Stringer; Rainer Grün; Qingfeng Shao; Katerina Harvati
item.description: Our current understanding of the origins of Homo sapiens is limited, in part, by the fragmented fossil record from Late Pleistocene and early Holocene Africa. Here, we re‐examine the Kabua 1 cranium, an enigmatic and little‐studied Kenyan fossil discovered in the 1950s. We compare virtual reconstructions created previously by our team with a wide range of Middle Pleistocene to Early Holocene fossils and recent African H. sapiens crania to assess Kabua 1's morphological affinities. We also provide a conservative new Uranium‐series minimum date of 64.4 ± 5.4 ka. Our results highlight Kabua 1's broad similarity to derived H. sapiens , both recent and fossil. Its morphology nevertheless demonstrates some more basal affinities and thus contributes to our understanding of the depth of phenotypic diversity in Late Pleistocene African H. sapiens .

item.title: Liquefying governmental dynamics: water politics in the waterless environments of the Kurdish regions of Turkey
item.dc:creator: Ibrahim Burhan Isik
item.description: Over the past twenty years, Turkey has undertaken a concerted effort to upgrade the country's infrastructure, covering a broad range of areas, including water, electricity, and housing. Despite the state's extensive infrastructural and architectural development projects, these upgrades have often resulted in more frequent and unpredictable disruptions such as prolonged water shortages rather than delivering the anticipated stability in infrastructure services, particularly in the predominantly Kurdish south‐eastern region. The instability of water distribution intensifies existing regional tensions and political discourses, as inadequate infrastructure has made water a pivotal component of the enduring tension between the Turkish state and the Kurdish people, particularly following the state's armed campaign in 2015. Through ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Mardin, a south‐eastern province of Turkey, this article investigates how governmental dynamics and local politics are shaped around the distribution of water, decisions regarding who has access to it, and the broader regional implications of these policies.

item.title: ‘Why didn't you bring us a pumpkin?’ Relational recognition of caste, class, and tribe in rural Andhra Pradesh, India
item.dc:creator: Thomas Herzmark
item.description: This article analyses the ways characteristics associated with the ‘Schedule Tribe’ (‘ST’) category in India shape situated acts of relating to others with either deference or assumed superiority. Ethnography shows how within an indigenous Adivasi community the traits that determine identification within the group generate feelings of entitlement and stigma, and provide frameworks for ascribing status distinctions to others, as equal, superior, or inferior. The ethnography of interaction between members of an ‘ST’ community captures the interpellative process of social actors continually placing each other into subjectively constituted maps of association and relatedness that are informed by longer discourses of classification. The material illuminates how characteristics associated with ‘ST’ identities that are valorized in one context may be stigmatized in another, suggesting that literatures on politics of recognition must be more attentive to the contextual variability of such frameworks in different spaces.

The material illuminates how characteristics associated with ‘ST’ identities that are valorized in one context may be stigmatized in another, suggesting that literatures on politics of recognition must be more attentive to the contextual variability of such frameworks in different spaces.

item.title: Liquidity, the makings of India's emerging economic body
item.dc:creator: Ikuno Naka
item.description: Under Narendra Modi's premiership, India's economy is rapidly being ‘dematerialized’ towards a digital economy: ‘faceless, paperless, cashless’ in his words. At first glance, it captures the quintessence of free laissez‐faire market reforms, but I argue there is more to Modi's project of liquidity. This paper re‐reads the re‐engineering of India's economy, arguing that this idea of liquidity is what holds together in conflicting tension the polarities for de‐regulated free laissez‐faire market reforms with a re‐sacralized and protectionist nationalism. Grounded in the stories of local builders working the ‘spatial fix’, the multi‐sited ethnography recovers how money is more than some medium of exchange or vessel for abstract value. It is itself constitutive of shared dispositions, meanings, understandings, a vernacular, all in service towards a conceived ideal commons. Reframing our understanding of modern money thus, the paper therefore argues that Modi's monetarist reforms are an assertion for a different kind of collective existence – a re‐sacralized socio‐spatial project wherein membership demands the reconfiguration of self and of relations, as these builders experience first‐hand. The economy is never just about economics; it is inherently political and indelibly personal.

item.title: ‘Collected photographs of naked women; left the RAI in mysterious circumstances, disowned by RAI’
item.dc:creator: Lisa Z. Sigel
item.description: This article reconstructs the history of E.N. Fallaize, a member of the Royal Anthropological Society and the British Association for the Advancement of Science, during the 1910s, 1920s, and 1930s, in order to assess his collection of mostly nude images. The collection exemplifies an uncomfortable ambiguity between ethnographic and pornographic images in the documentary record, the consideration of which makes visible an aspect of collecting and archiving visual images that has mostly been rendered opaque. It further explores the value of such collections, especially those associated with sexuality, at a critical moment in the history of archives, museums, and anthropology, because calls to de‐colonize anthropology have raised ethical and legal concerns about making such materials available for use.

item.title: Torture and scepticism in Papua New Guinea witch hunts
item.dc:creator: Chloe Nahum‐Claudel
item.description: For over a century, anthropologists have documented the many institutions that exist to respond to witchcraft and the uncanny that it names: oracles that attempt to produce certainty by naming the witch; moots in which grievances are aired; trials in magistrates’ courts that attempt to satisfy the community while preserving the life of the accused; Christian purification crusades that cleanse blackened souls to unify riven communities. But can the uncanny be contained by any of these institutions? Extending existing anthropological work on doubt and scepticism, I argue that the effort to know and contain witchcraft through ritual means is always premised on scepticism. It is a restless quest for conviction rather than a violent response to certainty. In the central highlands of Papua New Guinea today, self‐consciously modern witch trials involving torture have become the ultimate oracular authority for revealing and countering kumo witchcraft. Confessions made under torture seem to be uniquely satisfying, offering surer ‘proofs’ and ‘evidence’ in the place of indeterminate signs. However, alongside progressivist discourses, people denounce torture as abuse and point out the futility and hubris of seeking to know and contain witchcraft. Bringing together scholarship on witchcraft and scepticism from the anthropology of witchcraft (which has undertheorized torture) and work on torture and scepticism from history (which has extensively theorized torture), I argue that scepticism often redoubles violence in the pursuit of its resolution.

item.title: Mortal relationality: waria family care and the ethics of dying in Bali
item.dc:creator: Sylvia Tidey
item.description: Can a good death occur for those who balance on the edges of grievability? In Bali, where death marks a transition within the cycles of reincarnation, a good death depends on the mortuary care performed by intimate others – care that may be foreclosed to those whose lives are shaped by stigma. Through the death of Claudia, a Balinese Hindu waria (transgender woman) living with HIV, this article examines how dying well is inseparable from the ethical navigation of life. Drawing on long‐term ethnographic fieldwork on HIV/AIDS‐related care among gay and waria Indonesians, I ask when the relational, moral, and temporal labours of end‐of‐life care begin? Bringing anthropological studies of end‐of‐life care into conversation with existential philosophy, I develop the concept of mortal relationality to describe the ethical mode through which life and death are lived as a continuous moral project. For those dwelling at the margins of social recognition, the ‘choreography of death’ starts long before dying begins. And for them, a good life is not necessarily a long life but one in which a good death, with its relational implications, remains possible.

item.title: Conceptualizing moral migration: how disillusionment and the transnational right motivate migration to Russia
item.dc:creator: Lauren Woodard
item.description: Russia is consistently a top migration destination. While most migrate to Russia from other post‐Soviet countries, a small but highly visible group of the Russian‐speaking diaspora has returned from Europe and North America. Lauded in Russian media as ‘ideological migrants’, their narratives at first glance echo those of the state as they claim to flee liberalism and seek freedom. Drawing on ethnographic encounters with some of these migrants in Russia and the United States since 2014, this article examines how disillusionment and geopolitical imaginaries intersect with transnational circulations of the far right to motivate migration. Through two case studies of men returning from the West, this article conceptualizes their migration as a form of moral migration, an ethical alignment of where one lives with one's values. Ethnographic attention to moral migration has implications for understanding how individuals weigh factors beyond economic and political calculations to plan their migration and to address growing disillusionment worldwide with cultural and political liberalism.

item.title: Recent progress in studies of the last million years of human physical and behavioural evolution
item.dc:creator: James Cole; Eleanor M.L. Scerri; Mateja Hajdinjak; Chris Stringer
item.description: This article presents a synthesis of recent developments in the study of human evolution over the past five years. It begins with an overview of hominin species nomenclature and diversity, followed by an examination of the proposed population bottleneck ∼900,000 years ago. The discussion then turns to the ongoing debate regarding the Last Common Ancestor (LCA) of Homo sapiens , Neanderthals, and Denisovans, contextualized within patterns of hominin dispersal over the last million years. Key fossil discoveries, including Harbin, Homo luzonensis , Apidima 1, and Yunxian, are evaluated for their implications on evolutionary relationships. Finally, the paper explores recent findings related to hominin behaviour and considers their broader significance for understanding cognitive capacities in Middle to Late Pleistocene populations.
